doc.title: Peter Appleyard interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 4, 2012

title: Growing up in Cleethorpes: air raids, evacuation and butterfly bombs
summary: Born in Grimsby and raised in Cleethorpes, Appleyard recalls sleeping in an air raid shelter, evacuation to Wales, and the butterfly bombs, then leaving school at 13.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Great. Well I’m glad to have you here for this concert at Hamilton College. And I’ve been thinking of some things I wanted to ask you about. You’re from England.

Yes. I was born in a place called Grimsby, on the east coast of England. It was the largest commercial fishing port in England. And I was born there on a Tuesday and I didn’t like it. They moved me on a Wednesday down to a place called Cleethorpes, which is a place adjacent to it, a seaside resort.
And I lived there until I was, until I first went on the road. I think when I was 16, 17.
And you were a teenager during World War II?
What do you remember about that time?

I remember that I slept in an air raid shelter for three consecutive years. The first year I was evacuated to Wales because we were vulnerable, being a port. And they brought me © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-
back — nothing much happened for the first year — so they brought me back and it started, to a certain extent. I remember once seeing a flying bomb coming, you know?

No. They came too fast. This was a buzz bomb they called them. It was like a small jet plane. Something like the drones that you see today. And then they — Hitler had decided that he couldn’t demoralize the Londoners with these bombings, so he moved up to the provinces. And ours was one town where they experimented with a new anti-personnel bomb, called the butterfly bomb. And they would drop it, and it was about the size of a hand grenade. And it was a potent as a hand grenade. But when it fell it triggered a hairspring. It didn’t explode. But if you walked with six feet of it, it would blow up. I left school when I was 13, public school, and in those days in Britain you had to pay for a child’s secondary education, high school. But my parents were victims of the recession and didn’t have much money. They couldn’t afford to do that. And so they applied me for an apprenticeship for a compass adjuster and nautical instrument-maker.
